summary: Container is a tense closed-economy game (this is a new compact 2026 Allplay edition of the 2007 Franz-Benno Delonge/Thomas Ewert design, with Kevin Nesbitt credited on this release) where players manufacture, price, and auction shipping containers to each other rather than to a passive market. Playing it feels like running a cutthroat micro-economy — you're constantly reading opponents' secret value cards, undercutting their prices, and deciding when to sell versus hoard, and one badly-timed move can crash the whole market.
praised: Deep, believable closed-economy simulation where supply, demand, and pricing are entirely player-driven
High, meaningful interaction — buying low/selling high against real opponents, not a fixed market
Clever auction mechanic where the shipper can either take double the winning bid or buy the goods themselves, forcing tough calls
Hidden container-value cards create a deduction/bluffing layer as you try to read rivals' goals
Considered a genre-defining classic among economic gamers ('everyone trying to learn economics should be forced to play it')
criticised: Tight, unforgiving money supply can snowball badly for a player who falls behind early
Requires the full player count (game is much weaker or breaks down outside 3-5 players)
Steep initial learning curve to grasp market timing and pricing strategy
Some find the theme thin/abstract dressing over a pure economic engine

interaction.kind: direct player-to-player trading, price-setting, and auctioning off goods to (or against) rivals in a closed economy
interaction.detail: Money and containers only exist in fixed supply among the players, so every sale, price you set, or good you buy comes directly at another player's expense — you can undercut rivals' prices or refuse to buy their overpriced goods to squeeze them. Almost the whole game is the shared market and shared money pool rather than an independent personal board.
interaction.said: "cutthroat", "screw your neighbor", "brutal economy" — Container's reputation is built almost entirely around its nasty, adversarial market

sources: Money (cash held at game end, built up from selling containers/goods)
scoring.how_you_win: Players build factories and ships to produce and haul containers, trading them with each other and auctioning them at the harbor in a closed economy; when the game's goods or rounds run out, whoever holds the most cash wins.
scoring.score_note: final cash on hand, varies with player count/economy
